A cue of one second or less comes back as one event. Every first take that asked for two things in a row, a scrape then a slosh, a thud then crackling, came back as a single clink. A cue with two parts is asked for at 2.5 seconds or more and cut to its length by the chain.
The word glass at the head of a prompt gives a clink whatever else is asked. The next takes name the heavy thing and the stone first.
Hand, strokes and stir bring a spoon into the glass. The next shake take asks for a sealed jar.

An ambience prompt that names an instrument, bells, gets a passage of that instrument up close. The other seasons' ambience asks for one steady bed and names its distant detail as far away and sparse.

Ask for one real event that holds everything in the cue's line, never two events in a row: every take that named two things gave one of them. The third shake take named water in a bottle and a strap of sleigh bells and came back as bells alone.

A heavy thing named by its material and the surface it leaves, a stone mortar on a marble countertop, gave the first scrape that was heard as a heavy object leaving stone. Dragged and gritty, without the materials, gave animal grunts.

A tick asked for on wood, with no glass and no metal in the text, came back dull and under 1 kHz. The listener must hear a file under half a second with silence around it: the bare file was heard as a bell, the padded copy as a dry click.

A cue whose line holds two materials at once, liquid in glass and bells, did not come from one prompt in three takes. In a review round ask for the two layers as two cues and let the chain lay them together.
